title: Jeremiah 52:24–34
context: The narrator reports that Nebuzaradan took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, the threshold keepers, officials, and sixty men of the people of the land to Riblah, where the king of Babylon put them to death, then lists three deportations totaling four thousand six hundred people and closes with Evilmerodach releasing Jehoiachin in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, speaking kindly to him, and providing for him all his days. The executions parallel 2 Kings 25:18–21, the counts in 52:28–30 have no parallel in 2 Kings, and the release parallels 2 Kings 25:27–30, with these differences named without harmonizing. Both traditions read the executions soberly and the release as a quiet note of hope and shared ground, not a restored kingdom, and both may note, as a hedged option, that the line of David is not extinguished (cf. 2 Sam 7:16).

verses.text: The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold.” Arminian readers note that temple leaders are among those taken.

A Zephaniah the priest appears earlier in the book (cf. 21:1; 37:3).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the leadership of the temple removed.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, and both note the parallel in 2 Kings 25:18, without claiming more about these men than the text states.

verses.text: and out of the city he took an officer who was set over the men of war; and seven men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city; and the scribe of the captain of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the middle of the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list includes “an officer who was set over the men of war; and seven men of those who saw the king’s face.” Arminian readers note that civil and military leaders are taken.

Sixty men of the people of the land are included.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the leaders of the city’s resistance gathered for judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list plainly as the removal of Jerusalem’s remaining leadership, with the parallel in 2 Kings 25:19.

verses.text: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.” Arminian readers note that they are taken to the same place where Zedekiah was judged (52:9).

Riblah becomes a place of sentence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the pattern of judgment at Riblah.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse briefly and soberly, letting the narrator’s plain report stand.

verses.text: The king of Babylon struck them, and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Babylon struck them, and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath.” Arminian readers state the executions plainly and with grief.

The narrator adds, “So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse with sorrow, as the fulfillment of long-announced judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions refuse to expand on the violence, and both read the final sentence as the end of Judah’s life in the land.

verses.text: This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Jews;
verses.arminianNotes:
“This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Jews.” Arminian readers note that these figures have no parallel in 2 Kings.

How they relate to 2 Kings 24:12–16 is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the counts without forcing them into agreement with the larger numbers in 2 Kings 24:14–16.

Shared ground: both traditions read the figures as a sober record of real people carried into exile.

verses.text: in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty-two persons;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues: “in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty-two persons.” Arminian readers note this second deportation.

How the regnal years here relate to 52:12 and 2 Kings is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise record the number plainly and hold the reckoning lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that each figure stands for people uprooted from their homes, and both avoid harmonizing the dates.

verses.text: in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty-five people. All the people numbered four thousand six hundred.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list closes: “in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty-five people.” Arminian readers note a third deportation.

The total is “four thousand six hundred.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that this later deportation is not described elsewhere in the book.

Shared ground: both traditions read the totals soberly, and both note that what these numbers include is discussed rather than settled.

verses.text: In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, in the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evilmerodach king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and released him from prison.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah,” Evilmerodach “lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and released him from prison.” Arminian readers note the change in his fortunes.

2 Kings 25:27 gives the twenty-seventh day rather than the twenty-fifth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the release and the date difference without resolving it.

Shared ground: both traditions treat the release as a real kindness, but not a restoration of the kingdom.

verses.text: He spoke kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon,
verses.arminianNotes:
“He spoke kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon.” Arminian readers note the honor given to Jehoiachin among the exiled kings.

He remains in Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a measure of favor shown to the Davidic king in exile (cf. 1 Kings 8:50).

Shared ground: both traditions record the kindness without claiming that the kingdom is restored.

verses.text: and changed his prison garments. Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes:
Evilmerodach “changed his prison garments.” The narrator adds, “Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life.” Arminian readers note the change in his daily life.

He lives under the Babylonian king’s provision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a modest sign that the house of David is preserved.

Shared ground: both traditions note, as a hedged option, that the line of David is not extinguished (cf. 2 Sam 7:16), though the chapter does not develop the point.

verses.text: For his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him by the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him by the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death.” Arminian readers note the steady provision.

The book ends with the king still in exile.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the ending as restrained: no return and no restored throne, yet the Davidic king survives (cf. 2 Kings 25:27–30).

Shared ground: both traditions leave readers with a quiet note of continuity and hope, not a full restoration.
